title: Custom Hooks
summary: A custom Hook is a function that shares React behaviour between components.
introduction: A custom Hook is a function that shares React behaviour between components. When two parts repeat the same state steps, put those steps in a helper whose name starts with use. Each call still has its own state.
learningObjectives: State the rules of hooks and explain why they exist
Extract repeated stateful logic into a custom hook
Explain why two components using the same hook do not share state
Design a hook's return value for the way it will be used

blocks.text: React identifies each hook call by its **order** within a component. That gives two rules: call hooks only at the top level of a component or of another hook, never inside conditions, loops or nested functions; and call hooks only from React function components or custom hooks, not from ordinary JavaScript functions. The `use` function from React 19 is the one exception to the first rule.

A custom hook is any function whose name starts with `use` and that calls at least one hook. The prefix is not decoration: the `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` rules that the Vite template installs rely on it to know where to check the rules of hooks.

blocks.title: Breaking the first rule
ESLint
blocks.content: React Hook "useState" is called conditionally. React Hooks must be called in the exact same order in every component render. Did you accidentally call a React Hook after an early return?  (react-hooks/rules-of-hooks)

blocks.text: Nothing about the body changed; it was cut out of the component and pasted into a function. The component now reads like a sentence, and the subscription logic has one home where bugs get fixed once.

Each call to a custom hook gets its own state, exactly as two `useState` calls do. Two components using `useWindowWidth` each hold their own `width`; they happen to agree because both listen to the same window. The next example makes the independence visible.

blocks.text: If you *do* want several components to see the same value, the hook needs a shared source behind it: [context](/tutorials/react/context), an external store, or a server cache.

blocks.text: Returning `[value, setValue]` mirrors `useState`, so the hook is a drop-in replacement. The lazy initializer reads storage once; the effect writes on every change. Returning an array lets callers pick names; returning an object (as `useCounter` does) is better when there are more than two values or when callers rarely need all of them.

blocks.text: Because `url` is a dependency, switching from `<Todo id={1} />` to `<Todo id={2} />` fetches again, and the `ignore` flag discards any response that arrives for a URL that is no longer current. In production you would reach for a library that adds caching and retries, which the [data fetching lesson](/tutorials/react/data-fetching) covers; the hook is still worth understanding because that is what those libraries do inside.

blocks.title: Common mistake: a hook that is not named like one
blocks.text: Naming a helper `getWindowWidth` while it calls `useState` hides it from the lint rules, and calling it conditionally then corrupts the hook order with confusing errors such as "Rendered more hooks than during the previous render". Conversely, a function that calls no hooks should not be named `useX`; a plain name tells readers it can be called anywhere.

items: Name hooks after what they do for the component (`useOnlineStatus`), not how they do it (`useNavigatorOnLineEffect`).
Keep each hook focused; compose hooks from hooks when you need more.
Return exactly what callers use: a pair for one value and its setter, an object for several values.
Accept plain values as arguments and list them in the inner effect's dependencies, as `useFetch` does with `url`.

questions.question: Two components that both call `useCounter()` share the same `count` value.
questions.explanation: Every call to a hook creates its own state. Custom hooks share logic; to share state you need context, a store or a server cache.

questions.question: Why must a custom hook's name start with `use`?
questions.explanation: React itself does not check names, but the lint rules use the prefix to verify the rules of hooks inside the function, and readers immediately know it calls hooks.
options: React refuses to run functions with other names
So the lint rules can check the rules of hooks inside it and readers know it calls hooks
It makes the hook's state persist between renders
It is required for the hook to return an array

seo.title: React Custom Hooks – Reuse Stateful Logic
seo.description: Learn the rules of hooks and build custom hooks in React 19: useWindowWidth, useCounter, useLocalStorage and useFetch, plus advice on naming and return values.
